- @duckdb blazing fast columnar SQL. Simple API for loaders like csv, JSON, parquet, etc.

- @cohere, we built most of the engine using Cohere embeddings as we got lots of free credits. Great embeddings! Rooting for them.
- @OpenAI and PaLM of course, with excellent embeddings.
- @AlibabaGroup DAMO academy GTE embeddings. Tiny 22MB OSS embedding model with great performance (text embeddings have come so far in the last year)
- hsnw super fast in-memory vector store with a low-overhead py install
- @astral_sh Ruff is so fast and literally has saved us countless hours of eng time. Py tooling is so important.

title: Nikhil Thorat (@nsthorat)
summary:
Organized, manual inspection is critical for data quality.
At Google we found the silliest *bugs* from this process, ones that are very hard to fully automate beforehand:
- Rater instruction confusion: confusing “human race” with “running race”
- Question / Answer pairs swapped accidentally
- Labels leaking in images
Many other examples, but these are easy to fix once you’ve seen them, and often they dramatically boost model performance after being fixed.
Quoting @_jasonwei
One pattern I noticed is that great AI researchers are willing to manually inspect lots of data. And more than that, they build infrastructure that allows them to manually inspect data quickly. Though not glamorous, manually examining data gives valuable intuitions about the problem.
The canonical example here is Andrej Karpathy doing the ImageNet 2000-way classification task himself. And in the era of large language models, manually examining data is probably even more insightful since completions are hard to evaluate via benchmarks.
In this spirit, I recently did a few days of pair programming with @hwchung27 where we were starting on a new problem. Instead of trying to replicate baselines and design new methods, we ran some evaluations and manually inspected them to gain insights. We first paid about one day of overhead getting all the relevant information in a single UI so we could examine the data without having to click through multiple web pages. The second day, we spent an afternoon reading examples together and taking notes on the patterns that we noticed in the examples. ChatGPT generates long text, and we actually read the whole thing carefully, even if one example took 20 minutes to understand. I think we both gained a deeper understanding of the problem that we could not have gotten from reading research papers.
(In 2018, for example, I helped pathologists label a lot of data to train a lung cancer classifier. After having manually labeled 200+ images (with pathologist correction), I’d probably gained a pathologist-level understanding at that one particular lung cancer classification task :))

The incredible part of this LLM movement is the convergence around the simplest primitives: matmuls & nonlinearities.
There was a period of cambrian explosion of kernels / ops a few years ago, with subtle differences between frameworks (e.g. what do each of the dimensions of the conv kernel mean). New SOTA models had entirely different architectures.
This means it was insanely hard to standardize -- onnx is the only thing that pulled it off. But now we have GGUF/GGML.
When we worked on the WebNN spec, the hardest part was resolving these differences in one API, without losing performance, without a compiler, and *guaranteeing backward compatibility*. It now feels tractable, at least for language models.

Technology in general and AI in particular is not that predictable! People thought at one point that defeating human grandmasters at chess would probably take AGI! And that's not because they were stupid, it's because humanity didn't always know what we know now.
The history of which AI technology gets developed first is the history of which problems turned out to be surprisingly easy to solve by some algorithm that wouldn't obviously go that far. The history of disappointments? Wrong guesses about which algorithms do solve things. It wasn't stupid to guess we'd have robotic cars by now. I didn't make that guess, but I didn't say on the Internet that the other guess was stupid, because I didn't know, and neither did you.
Do you think you know better? Then say it in advance or nobody will or should believe you.
Say today what AI cannot do in 2025 that others think it can, say today what AI will do in 2025 that no industry leader expects. Bet now in the prediction markets or forever hold your peace.
Endpoints can sometimes be predicted but exact trajectories are hard.
Think you can do better? Think you could have predicted LLMs in 2016, or 2003, unlike me? I don't believe you until you prove it with an advance prediction record, and neither should anyone else.
The people who are like "lol MIRI didn't predict LLMs in 2003" are ignorant of history, and specifically that OpenAI and Deepmind didn't predict LLMs in 2016.
The people who are like "LLMs are so unlike what MIRI predicted!" are making a very closely related mistake, the mistake of thinking that we'd be confident enough to strongly predict which AI problems would be easiest to solve. We worked on a more abstract level and picked concrete examples that didn't sound stupid in 2013, knowing we didn't know exactly what would be possible in 2023. But some people are not abstract thinkers and can only ever imagine that, if I gave an example of optimization involving a malfunctioning time machine, I must have imagined AI to be exactly like that; while of course, they imagine, the average OpenAI employee was expecting ChatGPT.

Hot take — I finally *feel* the same visceral negative reaction visual artists had to midjourney.
Music is sacred to me because it is so fundamentally human.
For creators, it’s an artistic expression. For listeners, it’s a way to engage with other people — sharing music, finding artists they love, and dancing together.

I’ve always told people that when they dance, they’re creating. When they share a sick drop, they’re creating too.
To me, AI music that is completely end to end like this (text => music) completely destroys the point of music. Music is so far beyond language that trying to distill it to this feels like it’s completely missing the point. I fail to see how this is a good idea.

The best parallel I have to what I want to see in this AI music world is @runwayml. They don’t just say text => video, that’s super lame. Instead, they have AI powered tools that *empower* people creating videos, making them better at their job, and making folks who are video-artistic actually able to express themselves.

title: Nikhil Thorat (@nsthorat)
summary:
I imagine the right interface for AI assisted music production looks like 4 parts that you weave together in any order: generate, separate, refine, and stitch.
Advanced: There are ways to tag and reuse motifs. Motifs can be anything, raw audio, refinements, generations, evolution of effects over time.
This ideally should work for the “listeners” of music today who haven’t made a song.
1) generate parts of a song, either temporally (chorus) or stacked in time (the drums).
2) separate:
- basic stem removal
- text prompted + temporal selection stem removal “the airy part during the verse”
- refinement of the separation “less of the bass”, “you dropped the snare, bring that back!”
- maybe automatically regenerate diff stems during separation with a temperature knob
3) refinement, LOTS of cool ideas here. inspiration from @runwayml
Marry both opinionated things (standard effects, and AI powered effects), with text guided
- “motion brush” a part to give it more movement, you can still use text to guide
- “double the snare, build a big drop” and refine again “give space right before the 1” and “actually keep everything filtered out for a full bar after the 1”
- this is where you can get crazy, imagine you have a synplant2 type synth / effect that people are constantly can contribute data for (specifically text prompts of them, or manually patched and tagged with text).
4) stitch put it back together. You still have some way of seeing all the stems you’ve made.
Songs no longer have to be just an mp3 file, they could be an artifact that you can continue to evolve. Imagine you make a song for your kid to eat their food as @kavinstewart mentioned, but as they get older you continually refine it. It’s a beautiful artifact they have for their whole life they get to be nostalgic about, like an old drawing they made.
Quoting @samim
After extensive training with various music generation neural networks and dedicating countless hours to prompting them, it's become even more evident to me that relying solely on text prompts as interface for music creation significantly limits the creative process.

We're piloting the first service that I'm very excited about: LLM-powered & human-understandable dataset clustering!

title: Nikhil Thorat (@nsthorat)
summary:
It is *certainly* true that culture accounts for the /volume/ of success that immigrants have in STEM. And it’s certainly not the only predictor of success.
Growing up in the US as a second generation immigrant with an Indian father and American mother, I went to one of the better public high schools. What was “cool” in my high school was really important to what we cared about socially. Reading history books & going to after school math tutoring were things I was forced to do by my Indian father, and I put up a fight because it was cooler to play basketball & be funny around the popular kids and be “chill”.
My dad saw I was going down the “wrong path” (he caught me smoking pot with one of the cool kids) and sent me to a math and science school, something I despised him for at the time. In hindsight it was the best thing that ever happened to me academically — importantly because “cool” was suddenly redefined.
It was now cool to be smart, be in math club, hack the computers, make computer games. Competition was redefined from making funny jokes in class to solving some math problem before other people could.
At the same time, there are countless examples of people I’ve worked with who never had the culture of “smart”=“cool” and have gone on to be some of the most talented people in the field, completely self driven.
Overall, I think this point about culture is very strong. While it’s absolutely true you need to have a fire within you & have the self motivation to care about academic topics, what culture kids grow up in absolutely has profound effects on what they grow up to be. Kids don’t understand the trajectory they’re on, and culture / parental pushes can be key differentiators.
So I think it’s fair to say that the volume success from immigrants in STEM fields comes from some healthy blend of American culture and this other academic external push.
I don’t think it’s possible for this pendulum to swing too far into the other direction where we *only* focus on this type of tiger parenting (the exception is silicon valley, let’s focus on normal america), so I think this effort to shift this culture is a good one.
Quoting @VivekGRamaswamy
The reason top tech companies often hire foreign-born & first-generation engineers over “native” Americans isn’t because of an innate American IQ deficit (a lazy & wrong explanation). A key part of it comes down to the c-word: culture. Tough questions demand tough answers & if we’re really serious about fixing the problem, we have to confront the TRUTH:
Our American culture has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long (at least since the 90s and likely longer). That doesn’t start in college, it starts YOUNG.
A culture that celebrates the prom queen over the math olympiad champ, or the jock over the valedictorian, will not produce the best engineers.
A culture that venerates Cory from “Boy Meets World,” or Zach & Slater over Screech in “Saved by the Bell,” or ‘Stefan’ over Steve Urkel in “Family Matters,” will not produce the best engineers.
(Fact: I know *multiple* sets of immigrant parents in the 90s who actively limited how much their kids could watch those TV shows precisely because they promoted mediocrity…and their kids went on to become wildly successful STEM graduates).
More movies like Whiplash, fewer reruns of “Friends.” More math tutoring, fewer sleepovers. More weekend science competitions, fewer Saturday morning cartoons. More books, less TV. More creating, less “chillin.” More extracurriculars, less “hanging out at the mall.”
Most normal American parents look skeptically at “those kinds of parents.” More normal American kids view such “those kinds of kids” with scorn. If you grow up aspiring to normalcy, normalcy is what you will achieve.
Now close your eyes & visualize which families you knew in the 90s (or even now) who raise their kids according to one model versus the other. Be brutally honest.
“Normalcy” doesn’t cut it in a hyper-competitive global market for technical talent. And if we pretend like it does, we’ll have our asses handed to us by China.
This can be our Sputnik moment. We’ve awaken from slumber before & we can do it again. Trump’s election hopefully marks the beginning of a new golden era in America, but only if our culture fully wakes up. A culture that once again prioritizes achievement over normalcy; excellence over mediocrity; nerdiness over conformity; hard work over laziness.
That’s the work we have cut out for us, rather than wallowing in victimhood & just wishing (or legislating) alternative hiring practices into existence. I’m confident we can do it. 🇺🇸 🇺🇸

For the “AI eats software people” it’s useful to break things down into milestones.
Milestone 0: AI can translate very focused technical requirements into software.
Milestone 1: AI can translate project-scale technical requirements into software. This means understanding how many large technical components fit together.
Milestone 2: an AI translation layer of product requirements from a human to large scale technical requirements.
Milestone 3: AI coming up with product requirements altogether.
For humans, these are all pretty intermingled, and you need software engineers at all of these stages. I think it’s safe to assume you have to get to milestone 3 to “fully replace all software engineers”
I’m not sure if y’all have used LLMs in serious software engineering, but we’re not even at milestone 0 robustly. LLMs still completely screw up even when slightly complex technical constraints are well formed, in extremely subtle and frustrating ways.

title: Nikhil Thorat (@nsthorat)
summary:
As someone who cofounded a tech company in Boston and exited it, some thoughts:
- It’s plainly the case that you have to work 30% harder in Boston if you want to survive in deep tech, regardless of doing a startup or not. You will have to coordinate with California over zoom no matter what. You will miss critical facetime with folks on the west coast, so you should expect to travel to california often. Of course this is only if you are ambitious, there’s plenty of places to just cash out.
- VCs know that it’s much harder to do a startup in Boston, they will ask you to move to SF if they like you, or just twiddle their thumbs and remain “interested” without a yes.
- The VCs you want are on the west coast for early stage startups, again this means you need spend a lot more effort to convince them to join your round.
- I don’t think saying “start a company in Boston” is the solution to the macro problem.
- The macro problem is simply that the center of gravity isn’t here. Young people go to SF or NYC, these are usually folks you want to get in a startup. Usually they leave because of bigger opportunities there.
- To get out of the local minima of the center of gravity, there needs to be a concerted amount of energy the state / city need to put in to keep talent here. I don’t know exactly what it looks like, but maybe it’s giving some type of benefit to tech startups / tech companies for doing business here.
- It’s true that Boston is more amenable to affordable housing and good schools, this fundamentally means you will have a slightly older population of tech workers. This is awesome and I love it, but you need lots of young people too!
So why am I still in Boston? The weather sucks, there’s not a lot of deep tech here relatively speaking, and the art culture is pretty lacking here. The answer is that my family and friends are all here and I can afford to have a house here. But that’s barely a generalizable reason to make a thriving tech startup ecosystem.
I would love to see this city have a thriving tech ecosystem but I think this is a much bigger lift beyond just the will of individual founders.

The murder in Minneapolis by the government’s secret police this week has stirred something in me.
A mother was gunned down in the street by ICE, and the government doesn’t even have the decency to perform a scripted condolence. No matter which way the tires were pointing, this is a tragedy for her family, her children, and yet JD Vance, Palmer Lucky, and others instantly became the judge and the jury on twitter proclaiming the 37 year old white mother was a domestic terrorist and was trying to murder a federal officer; thus she *deserves* to be shot in the face. And you do too if you don’t comply.
Where is the humanity? How is everyone not terrified that this could happen to them, their mother, their sister? Isn’t it terrifying that the Vice President is immediately defending murder of american citizens?
I normally keep my politics quiet here because of how toxic twitter is and how annoying it can be to people who want a clean tech feed. Right now it just feels wrong not to say anything.
I haven’t quite been able to figure out the right words for how I feel. My first instinct is “fuck ICE” and “what the fuck is wrong with these people”. Those are my lizard brain reactions. But there’s something deeper that’s bothering me.
I can’t shake this feeling that the moral foundation that much of modern society stands upon is infected, and is festering. We teach kids that right and wrong exist, not to lie, that you don’t hurt people, and that you protect the vulnerable. And yet our highest elected officials encourage the burning and pillaging of these sacred lessons.
I could go on about how our current leadership just wants money and power, and they’re using immigrants as scapegoats to do so. Our economy is transforming rapidly, both with AI and because of greedy capitalist policies — the country is angry about legitimate things and democrats are not actually listening. Republicans are listening but are redirecting anger for their own power. The next 5 years are going to look a lot different because of technology; yet our heads are buried in the sand and we’re losing our way.
But maybe the only real thing we can do is to keep living and teaching the lessons of right and wrong, not to lie, that you don’t hurt people, and that you protect the vulnerable. Teach your kids these lessons in spite of Trump, Vance, Noem being lost beyond repair. Teach your kids that everyone deserves to be treated as a human being and not an object to be deported to a brutal prison cell.
I do believe that most people are still good, and that the best thing we can do to combat dehumanization by the government is more humanization of our neighbors. Go spend time with your republican cousins / neighbors and break bread with them. Don’t talk politics, play with their kids. Find common humanity.
But I don’t really have a call to action beyond this. I don’t really know what to do other than vote in November and refuse to pretend this is normal, publicly, even if it’s terrifying that you might get targeted and attacked. People in Nazi Germany stayed silent for this very fear, and we’re certainly living through a cosplay of that now.
The president called a 37 year old mother a domestic terrorist and that her 3 shots to the face by the gestapo was a tragedy of her own making.
The actual tragedy is that the Oval office propped up millions of people arguing about the direction of the tires of the car without having the humility to step back and ask if we want the government murdering civilians in broad daylight.
I am terribly sad for this country, our broken moral compass, and for hard working immigrants living in fear here. But I do believe we will eventually heal.
